    Integrating fast frequentist empirical-Bayes gene-expression dispersion estimation as a prior

    Stefano Mangiola

    Source: vignettes/dispersion-priors.Rmd
    dispersion-priors.Rmd

    Introduction on brmDE

    brmDE is a flexible tool capable of

    • mixed-effect models

    • non-parametric continuous smooth/spline models

    • alternative distributions such as NB and ZINB,

    brmDE fits one gene at a time to prioritise parallelisation. As a consequence, a single-gene likelihood cannot borrow strength across features, which is exactly what makes empirical-Bayes estimation of feature-wise negative-binomial dispersion useful when the number of replicates is small compared with the parameter size.

    Frequentist methods such as edgeR and DESeq2 estimate gene-wise dispersion through empirical Bayes very efficiently, although generally within more constrained fixed-effect model structures.

    The key idea is to establish the dispersion prior for brmDE cheaply with empirical Bayes. The beauty of this approach is that with enough information, the posterior can still move away from the empirical-Bayes estimated prior.

    The dispersion likelihood in the maximum-likelihood estimation is

    Lg(ϕ)=p(yg∣ϕ)L_g(\phi) = p(y_g\mid\phi)

    The edgeR weighted shared likelihood is not itself a Bayesian prior, but it can be used to define one. Conceptually:

    • The maximum of this weighted smoothed likelihood defines the mean of the prior.

    • The prior width is obtained from the local curvature of the weighted smoothed likelihood.

    From frequentist empirical Bayes smoothed shrunk likelihood to Bayesian dispersion prior

    Overall, our goal is to match the curvature of the smoothed shrunk (log)-likelihood (around its mode, because it is well behaved) to the curvature of the Bayesian prior, which is a Normal distribution (well behaved everywhere).

    • The curvature of the smoothed shrunk (log)-likelihood will be approximated with a quadratic, because it is well behaved around its mode.

    • The curvature of a normal distribution is 1/variance by definition.

    The following steps will go through this process in detail.

    Smoothed shrunk (log)-likelihood

    We take edgeR as an example.

    edgeR estimates an abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood and weights it through empirical Bayes. For gene gg,

    wℓsmooth,g(ϕ), w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi),

    where

    w=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗. w=\texttt{prior.n}.

    In brmDE, the dispersion parameter is handled on the log scale. We therefore define the prior kernel directly as a function of log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi):

    log⁡pg(log(ϕ))∝wℓsmooth,g(elog⁡(ϕ)). \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) \propto w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}\left(e^{\log(\phi)}\right).

    The maximum of this prior kernel occurs at

    log⁡(ϕtrend,g), \log\left(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}\right),

    where ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} is returned by edgeR as trended.dispersion.

    We use the local shape of the log likelihood around its mode, to define the SD of the brmDE prior of log phi.

    Intuitive route from weighted smoothed likelihood to prior SD:

    1. Treat the weighted smoothed curve as an unnormalised log-density on the log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi) scale.
    2. Exponentiate it to obtain an unnormalised probability density.
    3. Normalise it so that its total area is 1.
    4. Calculate the mean and SD of that probability distribution.
    5. Equivalently, one could sample from the normalised density and calculate the empirical SD.
    6. A faster local approximation is to estimate the SD from the curvature around the mode.

    Why curvature can be calculated directly from the weighted log-likelihood

    We are calculating the curvature of the log of the weighted normalised probability density, as a proxy for the curvature of the prior density itself, prior in this case being likelihood * weight.

    Define the weighted smoothed log-likelihood on the log-dispersion scale as

    qg(log(ϕ))=wℓsmooth,g(elog⁡(ϕ)). q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}\left(e^{\log(\phi)}\right).

    The corresponding normalised prior density can be written as

    pg(log(ϕ))=exp⁡[qg(log(ϕ))]Z, p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = \frac{ \exp\left[ q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) \right] }{ Z },

    where ZZ is the normalising constant.

    Taking the logarithm gives

    log⁡pg(log(ϕ))=qg(log(ϕ))−log⁡Z. \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right)-\log Z.

    Since log⁡Z\log Z is constant with respect to log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi),

    d2d[log⁡(ϕ)]2log⁡pg(log(ϕ))=d2d[log⁡(ϕ)]2qg(log(ϕ)). \frac{d^2}{d[\log(\phi)]^2} \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = \frac{d^2}{d[\log(\phi)]^2} q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right).

    The curvature of the edgeR likelihood

    The smoothed shared log-likelihood is available numerically over a dispersion candidate range, evaluated at chosen candidate values within that range, so we estimate its local curvature from those candidate values.

    Suppose there are GG genes and KK candidate dispersion values.

    • shared.loglik is a G×KG \times K matrix. Rows correspond to genes and columns correspond to candidate dispersion values.
    • shared.loglik[g, ] is therefore a numeric vector of length KK. It gives the y-values of the abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood for gene gg across candidate dispersions.
    • spline.pts is a numeric vector of length KK. It gives the candidate-value coordinates corresponding to the KK columns of shared.loglik.
    • prior.n is the weight applied to the shared likelihood. In the standard non-robust case it is a scalar; with robust estimation it may be gene-specific.

    The x-axis used for the local fit is

    xk=log⁡(ϕk). x_k = \log(\phi_k).

    The corresponding y-axis is

    yk=wg×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔[g,k], y_k = w_g \times \texttt{shared.loglik}[g,k],

    where wgw_g is prior.n for gene gg when gene-specific weights are used, or the common scalar prior.n otherwise.

    Thus, for gene gg, the local fit uses the paired points

    (xk,yk)=(log(ϕk),wg×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔[g,k]). \left( x_k, y_k \right) = \left( \log(\phi_k), \; w_g \times \texttt{shared.loglik}[g,k] \right).

    Local quadratic fit

    Rather than trying to derive a probability distribution from the smoothed shrunk likelihood and sample from it to get the standard deviation, we use an approximate method.

    We estimate the curvature around the expected mode, which tends to be quadratic in shape.

    xtrend,g=log⁡(ϕtrend,g). x_{\mathrm{trend},g} = \log\left(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}\right).

    We select a small number of candidate values around the candidate closest to xtrend,gx_{\mathrm{trend},g} and define

    zk=xk−xtrend,g. z_k = x_k - x_{\mathrm{trend},g}.

    Since the smooth likelihood around its maximum tends to be quadratic in shape, we then fit the local quadratic model

    yk=a+bzk+czk2. y_k = a + b z_k + c z_k^2.

    This can be fitted directly with base R stats::lm() because the model is linear in the coefficients aa, bb, and cc.

    In R, the design formula is

    y[idx] ~ z + I(z^2)

    where

    z <- x[idx] - log(phi_trend_g)

    and idx identifies a small neighbourhood of candidate values around the trended dispersion.

    The fitted design matrix has three columns:

    interceptzz211z1z1221z2z22⋮⋮⋮⋮n1znzn2 \begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{intercept} & z & z^2\\ \hline 1 & 1 & z_1 & z_1^2\\ 2 & 1 & z_2 & z_2^2\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ n & 1 & z_n & z_n^2 \end{array}

    and lm() estimates

    a,b,c. a,\;b,\;c.

    The fitted function is therefore a parabola.

    The second derivative of the fitted quadratic is

    d2dz2(a+bz+cz2)=2c. \frac{d^2}{dz^2} \left( a+bz+cz^2 \right) = 2c.

    At a valid local maximum,

    c<0. c<0.

    From a parabola to the curvature

    The local curvature of a parabola is defined as:

    Ig=−2c. I_g = -2c.

    A sharper peak gives larger positive curvature,

    sharp peak⇒Ig large, \text{sharp peak} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_g\text{ large},

    whereas a flatter peak gives smaller curvature,

    flat peak⇒Ig small. \text{flat peak} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_g\text{ small}.

    Convert curvature into a brms prior standard deviation

    Matching the curvature of the parabola to the curvature of a Normal distribution, we can derive the SD of the Normal distribution.

    For a Normal distribution,

    log⁡p(x)=C−(x−μ)22σ2, \log p(x) = C - \frac{ (x-\mu)^2 }{ 2\sigma^2 },

    so its curvature at the mode is

    1σ2. \frac{1}{\sigma^2}.

    Matching the Normal curvature to the local quadratic fit gives

    Ig=1σg2. I_g = \frac{1}{\sigma_g^2}.

    Since

    Ig=−2c, I_g=-2c,

    the prior variance is

    σg2=−12c. \sigma_g^2 = -\frac{1}{2c}.

    Therefore the local Normal approximation for the brmDE log-dispersion prior is

    log⁡(ϕg)≈N(log(ϕtrend,g),−12cg) \log(\phi_g) \approx N\left( \log(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}), -\frac{1}{2c_g} \right)

    with

    cg<0. c_g<0.

    The centre of the prior therefore comes from trended.dispersion, while its width is derived from the local curvature of the weighted shared edgeR likelihood.

    estimate_dispersion_prior() writes two columns: dispersion_prior_log_mean (trended.dispersion) and dispersion_prior_log_sd (a width on log⁡ϕ\log\phi from the local quadratic of the weighted shared log-likelihood).

    Appendix 1: edgeR calculation of the smoothed weighted likelihood

    Disclaimer: the following section should not be taken as a substitute for the official edgeR literature (see references). It is just a convenient complement. For any divergence, the official literature should be considered instead.

    1. Each gene has a likelihood curve over candidate dispersions

    For gene gg, with observed counts ygy_g, edgeR evaluates the negative-binomial likelihood

    Lg(ϕ)=p(yg∣ϕ). L_g(\phi) = p(y_g\mid\phi).

    Usually we work with the log-likelihood

    ℓg(ϕ)=log⁡p(yg∣ϕ). \ell_g(\phi) = \log p(y_g\mid\phi).

    The data ygy_g are fixed, while ϕ\phi varies over candidate dispersion values within a chosen range,

    ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕK. \phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\phi_K.

    Across genes, this produces a matrix such as

    ϕ1ϕ2ϕ3ϕ4g1ℓ1(ϕ1)ℓ1(ϕ2)ℓ1(ϕ3)ℓ1(ϕ4)g2ℓ2(ϕ1)ℓ2(ϕ2)ℓ2(ϕ3)ℓ2(ϕ4)g3ℓ3(ϕ1)ℓ3(ϕ2)ℓ3(ϕ3)ℓ3(ϕ4) \begin{array}{c|cccc} & \phi_1 & \phi_2 & \phi_3 & \phi_4\\ \hline g_1 & \ell_1(\phi_1) & \ell_1(\phi_2) & \ell_1(\phi_3) & \ell_1(\phi_4)\\ g_2 & \ell_2(\phi_1) & \ell_2(\phi_2) & \ell_2(\phi_3) & \ell_2(\phi_4)\\ g_3 & \ell_3(\phi_1) & \ell_3(\phi_2) & \ell_3(\phi_3) & \ell_3(\phi_4) \end{array}

    Each row is one gene-specific log-likelihood curve over ϕ\phi.

    2. edgeR smooths each dispersion column over abundance

    Each gene has an abundance value AgA_g.

    For one fixed candidate dispersion ϕk\phi_k, edgeR has the log-likelihood values

    ℓ1(ϕk),ℓ2(ϕk),…,ℓG(ϕk). \ell_1(\phi_k), \ell_2(\phi_k), \ldots, \ell_G(\phi_k).

    It smooths these values against abundance:

    Ag→ℓg(ϕk). A_g \longrightarrow \ell_g(\phi_k).

    With the default edgeR implementation, this smoothing uses local regression through locfit.

    For every fixed candidate dispersion ϕk\phi_k, edgeR therefore obtains a smooth function of abundance, fk(A)f_k(A).

    3. For one abundance, reconstruct the smoothed log-likelihood curve over dispersion

    Consider a particular gene gg with abundance AgA_g.

    For every candidate dispersion,

    ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕK, \phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\phi_K,

    edgeR evaluates the corresponding abundance-smoothed function at AgA_g:

    f1(Ag),f2(Ag),…,fK(Ag). f_1(A_g), f_2(A_g), \ldots, f_K(A_g).

    These values are placed side by side across dispersion:

    ϕϕ1ϕ2⋯ϕKsmoothed log-likelihoodℓsmooth,g(ϕ1)ℓsmooth,g(ϕ2)⋯ℓsmooth,g(ϕK) \begin{array}{c|cccc} \phi & \phi_1 & \phi_2 & \cdots & \phi_K\\ \hline \text{smoothed log-likelihood} & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_1) & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_2) & \cdots & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_K) \end{array}

    Together, these values define the function

    ℓsmooth,g(ϕ). \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    This corresponds to edgeR’s internal notation m0g(ϕ)m_{0g}(\phi); for clarity, we use ℓsmooth,g(ϕ)\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) throughout.

    In the edgeR implementation:

    • trended.dispersion is returned by estimateDisp() and gives the abundance-dependent dispersion trend;
    • m0 is the internal matrix of local shared log-likelihoods;
    • prior.n is the weight applied to the shared likelihood contribution;
    • tagwise.dispersion is the final gene-specific moderated dispersion estimate.

    4. The maximum of this curve gives the trended dispersion

    edgeR finds the dispersion value at which the smoothed log-likelihood is maximal:

    ϕtrend,g=arg⁡maxϕℓsmooth,g(ϕ). \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} = \arg\max_{\phi} \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    Thus ℓsmooth,g(ϕ)\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) is the whole curve, whereas ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} is one value of ϕ\phi: the dispersion preferred by the across-gene information for a gene with abundance AgA_g.

    Repeating this operation over abundance produces the dispersion-abundance trend,

    A→ϕtrend(A). A \longrightarrow \phi_{\mathrm{trend}}(A).

    5. edgeR weights the across-gene log-likelihood curve

    We explain the derivation of prior.df in a generative fashion.

    What is fixed and already calculated:

    • dgd_g comes from the design
    • ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} from the abundance smooth.

    What are the master unknown parameters from where everything else is generated:

    • The location of the residual deviance s02s_0^2
    • The tightness around the location, depending on degrees of freedom d0d_0. Large d0d_0 leads to high tightness

    Step 1. Draw the gene’s true residual variance. Not all genes will have the same dispersion deviance (from the common trend ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}), for biological reasons. So each one is given its own true residual variance σg2\sigma_g^2, drawn from a scaled inverse chi-square centred on s02s_0^2:

    σg2∼d0s02χd02. \sigma_g^2 \;\sim\; \frac{ d_0\,s_0^2 }{ \chi^2_{d_0} }.

    Step 2. Draw the observed deviance ratio around it. Given that latent truth, the actual dispersion deviance we observe sg2s_g^2 is drawn from a distribution, defined by σg2\sigma_g^2.

    sg2∣σg2∼σg2χdg2dg. s_g^2\mid\sigma_g^2 \;\sim\; \frac{ \sigma_g^2\,\chi^2_{d_g} }{ d_g }.

    Eliminate σg2\sigma_g^2. We substitute step 1 into step 2 and the latent σg2\sigma_g^2 is integrated out:

    sg2=d0s02χd02⋅χdg2dg=d0s02dg⋅χdg2χd02. s_g^2 \;=\; \frac{ d_0\,s_0^2 }{ \chi^2_{d_0} } \cdot \frac{ \chi^2_{d_g} }{ d_g } \;=\; \frac{ d_0\,s_0^2 }{ d_g } \cdot \frac{ \chi^2_{d_g} }{ \chi^2_{d_0} }.

    The two chi-squares are independent, because step 1 draws σg2\sigma_g^2 before the counts of step 2 are realised. A ratio of independent chi-squares, each over its own degrees of freedom, is exactly an FF:

    sg2∼s02Fdg,d0, s_g^2 \;\sim\; s_0^2\,F_{d_g,\,d_0},

    with s02s_0^2 as pure scale and the two degrees of freedom as shape. So the observed vector is marginally a scaled FF sample, and no gene’s σg2\sigma_g^2 is ever computed. Fitting that FF is the whole job, and it is fitFDist() inside squeezeVar().

    How s02s_0^2 and d0d_0 are recovered

    s02s_0^2 enters only as a multiplicative scale, so on the log scale it is a shift. d0d_0 enters through the spread of the FF. And dgd_g is already known. They are not solved jointly, but sequentially.

    Taking logs and using 𝔼[logχd2]=ψ(d/2)+log⁡2\mathbb{E}\left[\log\chi^2_d\right]=\psi(d/2)+\log 2 and Var[logχd2]=ψ′(d/2)\mathrm{Var}\left[\log\chi^2_d\right]=\psi'(d/2) gives one equation for each:

    Var[logsg2]=ψ′(dg/2)⏟sampling noise+ψ′(d0/2)⏟between-gene spread, \mathrm{Var}\left[\log s_g^2\right] = \underbrace{\psi'(d_g/2)}_{\text{sampling noise}} + \underbrace{\psi'(d_0/2)}_{\text{between-gene spread}},

    𝔼[logsg2]=log⁡s02+[ψ(dg/2)−log(dg/2)]−[ψ(d0/2)−log(d0/2)]. \mathbb{E}\left[\log s_g^2\right] = \log s_0^2 + \left[\psi(d_g/2)-\log(d_g/2)\right] - \left[\psi(d_0/2)-\log(d_0/2)\right].

    The variance equation contains d0d_0 alone, because a scale factor cannot change a variance of logs, so s02s_0^2 has dropped out of it. That is what lets d0d_0 be recovered first: subtract the known sampling term and invert the trigamma,

    ψ′(d0/2)=Var̂[logsg2]−ψ′(dg/2),d0=2ψ′−1(⋅), \psi'(d_0/2) = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\left[\log s_g^2\right] - \psi'(d_g/2), \qquad d_0 = 2\,\psi'^{-1}\!\left(\cdot\right),

    which limma evaluates with trigammaInverse().

    Then, the mean equation gives log⁡s02\log s_0^2, since it needs d0d_0 through its digamma term.

    This technique is called moment matching, which is a substitute for maximum likelihood.

    From d0d_0 to the weight ww

    edgeR reports d0d_0 as prior.df. Dividing one by the other expresses the shared across-gene information,

    w=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚍𝚏𝚗𝚕𝚒𝚋𝚜−𝚗𝚌𝚘𝚎𝚏𝚜. w = \frac{ \texttt{prior.df} }{ \texttt{nlibs}-\texttt{ncoefs} }.

    So prior.n =2=2 means the across-gene trend carries twice as much information as the gene’s own counts, and prior.n =0.5=0.5 means half as much.

    Appendix 2: Where edgeR’s dispersion and the brms shape differ

    The design. estimateDisp() fits a fixed-effects GLM, so a random-effect term has to be handled somehow, and the two available choices bias ϕg\phi_g in opposite directions. Stripping it, for example passing ~ dex while brms fits ~ dex + (1 | cell), brings between-cell variance to ϕg\phi_g, inflating it. Passing the fixed-effect analogue (~ dex + cell) estimates those cell effects without shrinkage, so they absorb more variance than the mixed model’s partially pooled ones will, leaving ϕg\phi_g below the conditional shape brms is going to estimate. The target sits between the two:

    ϕedgeR(∼dex+cell)≤ϕbrmsconditional≤ϕedgeR(∼dex), \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex}\,+\,\mathrm{cell})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}} \;\le\; \phi^{\mathrm{conditional}}_{\mathrm{brms}} \;\le\; \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}},

    with the position depending on how hard the mixed model shrinks, which is not known before fitting.

    The fixed-effect analogue also costs residual degrees of freedom. On airway’s 8 samples, ~ dex + cell spans 5 columns and leaves d=3d=3, whereas ~ dex leaves d=6d=6. This reduction in residual degrees of freedom increases the sampling uncertainty of the gene-wise residual dispersion estimates and can therefore affect the empirically estimated d0d_0. Because d0d_0 sets prior.n, and prior.n weights the shared curve whose curvature becomes the prior width, the choice of fixed-effect approximation can indirectly change that width.

    The family. The default is zero-inflated negative binomial. shape there is the same parameter as in negbinomial(), with the same NB kernel and the same log link; what differs is the estimand. It describes the count component, whereas edgeR fits a plain negative binomial to the marginal counts.

    Zero inflation contributes overdispersion quadratic in μ\mu exactly as the NB dispersion does, so a marginal fit sees the two combined. Matching Var(Y)=E[Y]+ϕE[Y]2\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathrm{E}[Y] + \phi\,\mathrm{E}[Y]^2 against the zero-inflated moments gives

    ϕmarginal=ϕ+π1−π,π=𝚣𝚒, \phi_{\mathrm{marginal}} = \frac{\phi+\pi}{1-\pi}, \qquad \pi=\texttt{zi},

    which pins both the direction and the size of that mismatch. edgeR’s estimate exceeds the ZINB component’s ϕ\phi whenever π>0\pi>0, by roughly π\pi in absolute terms and π/ϕ\pi/\phi in relative terms, so genes with small dispersion are the most distorted. The same expression is why zi and shape are only weakly separated: the mean-variance relationship constrains the combination, not the pair, leaving the shape of the zero mass as the main information that distinguishes them.

    The Student-t prior confers robstness to misrepresentation of dispersion prior estimates

    There are two important situations in which the edgeR dispersion trend can be systematically displaced from the dispersion estimated by brmDE (see Appendix 2).

    • Because edgeR dispersion estimation cannot fit mixed-effects models, a mixed-effects brmDE model must be approximated by a fixed-effects model. For example, ~ treatment + (1 | hospital) may be approximated by ~ treatment + hospital. The fixed effects are estimated without partial pooling and can absorb more variation, potentially reducing the residual negative-binomial dispersion.

    • A zero-inflated negative-binomial model in brmDE must be approximated upstream by an ordinary negative-binomial model. Zero inflation can then be absorbed by the edgeR negative-binomial dispersion, potentially increasing the estimated dispersion.

    Student-t has heavier tails, so the gene-wise posterior can leave a misplaced edgeR mode when the likelihood disagrees. The default width still comes from the local curvature of the weighted shared log-likelihood.

    Appendix 3: Examples of how to use R formulas to approximate a mixed-effect model with a fixed-effect one

    edgeR and DESeq2 have no random effects. Pass estimate_dispersion_prior() the fixed-effect analogue of the mixed model you will fit in brmDE: drop the | and promote the grouping factor to a fixed term. If the random term also has a slope, include the interaction.

    Mixed-effect model (brmDE) Fixed-effect analogue
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) ~ treatment + hospital
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) + (1 \| batch) ~ treatment + hospital + batch
    ~ treatment + (treatment \| hospital) ~ treatment * hospital

    The last row is the random-slope case: (treatment | hospital) is (1 + treatment | hospital), so the analogue needs hospital-specific intercepts and hospital-specific treatment effects, which is treatment * hospital.

    Do not expand a nested random intercept (1 | hospital/ward) as hospital / ward. That formula is hospital + hospital:ward, which is rank-deficient when every ward belongs to one hospital, and edgeR will not fit it. Use the innermost grouping instead, uniquely coded: ~ treatment + ward.

    Illustration: the local quadratic approximation on airway

    The prior width from estimate_dispersion_prior() treats edgeR’s weighted, abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood as an unnormalised log-density on log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi), and replaces it with a Normal whose SD matches the local curvature at the mode. That is a local quadratic, not a claim that the whole curve is Gaussian.

    Below, airway is filtered and the design is the fixed-effect analogue of ~ dex + (1 | cell). The black curves are y=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔y = \texttt{prior.n}\times\texttt{shared.loglik}; the dashed line is log⁡(𝚝𝚛𝚎𝚗𝚍𝚎𝚍.𝚍𝚒𝚜𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗)\log(\texttt{trended.dispersion}); the orange curve is the Laplace Normal N(log⁡ϕtrend,σ2)N(\log\phi_{\mathrm{trend}},\sigma^2) fitted locally around that mode.

    # Build the design, drop low-count genes, and run edgeR's own dispersion
# estimation. estimateDisp() supplies prior.n, trended.dispersion, AveLogCPM
# and the plotBCV input used below.
library(edgeR)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(ggplot2)

data("airway", package = "airway")

design <- model.matrix(~ dex + cell, data = as.data.frame(colData(airway)))

dge <- DGEList(assay(airway, "counts"))
dge <- dge[filterByExpr(dge, design), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dge <- normLibSizes(dge)
dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design)
    # estimateDisp() does not return the shared log-likelihood, so rebuild it:
# Cox--Reid adjusted profile likelihood at each candidate phi, then smooth
# each candidate column against abundance with WLEB.
spline.pts <- seq(-20, 10, length.out = 61)   # wider and finer than edgeR's default
phi <- 0.1 * 2^spline.pts
x <- log(phi)

# Each fit starts from the previous candidate's coefficients; this is what
# estimateDisp() does internally, and the curves are poorly converged without it.
l0 <- matrix(0, nrow(dge), length(phi))
last.beta <- NULL
for (i in seq_along(phi)) {
  out <- adjustedProfileLik(
    phi[[i]],
    y = dge$counts,
    design = design,
    offset = getOffset(dge),
    start = last.beta,
    get.coef = TRUE
  )
  l0[, i] <- out$apl
  last.beta <- out$beta
}

shared.loglik <- WLEB(
  theta = spline.pts,
  loglik = l0,
  covariate = dge$AveLogCPM,
  trend.method = "locfit",
  overall = FALSE,
  individual = FALSE,
  m0.out = TRUE
)$shared.loglik
    # Abundance-dispersion trend: points are tagwise BCV = sqrt(phi),
# the line is trended.dispersion, the mode of the curves plotted next.
plotBCV(dge)

    # Take 25 genes evenly spaced in abundance, weight each shared curve by
# prior.n, and fit the local quadratic around log(trended.dispersion) to
# get sigma = sqrt(-1 / (2c)).
idx <- order(dge$AveLogCPM)[round(seq(1, nrow(dge), length.out = 25))]
Y <- rep_len(dge$prior.n, nrow(dge))[idx] * shared.loglik[idx, , drop = FALSE]
x_mode <- log(dge$trended.dispersion[idx])

sigma <- vapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
  i0 <- which.min(abs(x - x_mode[[i]]))
  j <- max(1L, i0 - 4L):min(length(x), i0 + 5L)
  z <- x[j] - x_mode[[i]]
  c_hat <- coef(lm(Y[i, j] ~ z + I(z^2)))[[3L]]
  sqrt(-1 / (2 * c_hat))
}, numeric(1))

panel <- sprintf(
  "%s\nlogCPM = %.1f\nσ = %.2f",
  rownames(dge)[idx],
  dge$AveLogCPM[idx],
  sigma
)

curve_df <- data.frame(
  gene = factor(rep(panel, each = length(x)), levels = panel),
  log_phi = rep(x, times = length(idx)),
  y = as.vector(t(Y))
)

# The parabola is drawn on a finer x than the 61 candidates, and clipped to the
# range of the curve so a diverging tail cannot flatten the free y scales.
x_fine <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 201)
normal_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
  y0 <- Y[i, which.min(abs(x - x_mode[[i]]))]
  y_n <- y0 - (x_fine - x_mode[[i]])^2 / (2 * sigma[[i]]^2)
  keep <- y_n >= min(Y[i, ], na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    gene = factor(panel[[i]], levels = panel),
    log_phi = x_fine[keep],
    y = y_n[keep]
  )
}))

mode_df <- data.frame(gene = factor(panel, levels = panel), log_phi_trend = x_mode)

ggplot(curve_df, aes(log_phi, y)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "edgeR weighted shared log-likelihood")) +
  geom_line(data = normal_df, aes(colour = "Laplace Normal"), linetype = 22) +
  geom_vline(
    data = mode_df,
    aes(xintercept = log_phi_trend),
    linetype = 2,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "edgeR weighted shared log-likelihood" = "black",
    "Laplace Normal" = "#d95f02"
  )) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5) +
  labs(x = expression(log(phi)), y = "prior.n × shared.loglik", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    strip.text = element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
